extracted.intended_audience: editors, researchers, funders, academic institutions, and other scholarly publishing stakeholders
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether a scholarly journal or publisher is predatory or a pseudo-journal, using multiple indicators (Beall’s criteria, DOAJ seal criteria, Think.Check.Submit. checklist, and warning signs) and a cumulative red-flag approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does not provide external peer review / publishes most submissions without review
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishes all or most submitted material without external peer review, despite claims of peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The hallmark of traditional scholarly publishing is external peer review; journals that mimic peer review but publish without it are predatory/pseudo-journals. Check submission-to-publication workflows and evidence of genuine peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims peer review but lacks real review processes
rubrics_metrics.description: The journal claims to conduct peer review yet provides no evidence that reviews are external, substantive, or competent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for descriptions of peer review type, reviewer identities/affiliations (when appropriate), review timelines, and examples of reviewer reports if available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequent mass solicitations for submissions promising rapid publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Sends frequent e-mails to large numbers of individuals soliciting manuscript submission and promising rapid publication for author fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulaic, generic solicitations that do not reference an author's work or specialty are a red flag; promised turnaround times that are unrealistically short also indicate risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collects author fees but fails to publish articles or deliver promised services
rubrics_metrics.description: Takes publication fees yet the promised published articles never appear or services (indexing, archiving) are not provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify fee transparency and evidence of previously published content; look for surprise invoices after submission as an indicator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-adherence to accepted publishing standards and policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Does not follow standard policies advocated by organizations (WAME, COPE, ICMJE, CSE) on archiving, conflict-of-interest management, errata, and transparency of processes and fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for clear policies on archiving/digital preservation, conflict of interest disclosure, corrections/retractions, and transparent fee information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mimics legitimate journal structure to appear authentic
rubrics_metrics.description: Mimics website and organizational structure of legitimate journals (e.g., editorial pages, article layout) without providing genuine editorial processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether named structures (editorial board, instructions for authors) correspond to verifiable people and processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uses counterfeit or misleading metrics and fake impact factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Falsely claims Thomson-Reuters (or other legitimate) impact factors, advertises impact factors assigned by fake services, or uses made-up metrics (e.g., 'view factor').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify any claimed metrics against recognized indexing/metric providers and be wary of unfamiliar metric names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor and staff: owner is editor of every journal
rubrics_metrics.description: The publisher's owner is identified as the editor of each and every journal published by the organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Single-person control of many journals is suspicious—check for independent editorial leadership for each journal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor and staff: no specific individual identified as journal editor
rubrics_metrics.description: No single individual is identified as any specific journal's editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legitimate journals normally list an editor-in-chief or comparable leader; absence suggests weak governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor and staff: no formal editorial/review board identified
rubrics_metrics.description: The journal does not identify a formal editorial/review board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial boards should be listed with affiliations and roles; lack of such a board is a red flag.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor and staff: no academic information for editors/staff
rubrics_metrics.description: No academic information is provided regarding the editor, editorial staff, and/or review board members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for verifiable institutional affiliations and academic credentials for editorial personnel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor and staff: editorial/review board lacks academic expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence exists showing that the editor and/or review board members do not possess academic expertise to reasonably qualify them as publication gatekeepers in the journal's field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check members' publication records and positions to confirm relevant expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor and staff: duplicate editorial boards across journals
rubrics_metrics.description: Two or more journals have duplicate editorial boards (i.e., same editorial board for more than one journal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identical boards across multiple titles often indicate template-driven, low-quality operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor and staff: insufficient or fabricated board members
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals have an insufficient number of board members (e.g., 2 or 3), concocted editorial boards (made up names), list scholars without their knowledge, or include prominent researchers who contribute only their name/photo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contact listed members (or check their websites) to confirm affiliation; very small boards are suspicious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor and staff: little or no geographic diversity on editorial board
rubrics_metrics.description: There is little or no geographical diversity among editorial board members, especially for journals that claim to be international in scope or coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Low diversity alone is not proof of predatory practice (may affect LMIC journals), but is a potential indicator when combined with other red flags.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor and staff: gender bias on editorial board
rubrics_metrics.description: The editorial board engages in gender bias (i.e., exclusion of any female members).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This may signal poor governance or bias; WAME notes such criteria alone are unreliable indicators of predatory status but warrant consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business management: lack of transparency in operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrates a lack of transparency in publishing operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparent contact info, policies, fee schedules, and organizational details are expected for legitimate journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business management: no digital preservation policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Has no policies or practices for digital preservation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legitimate journals have archiving strategies (e.g., CLOCKSS, Portico) or deposit policies; absence risks loss of scholarly record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business management: launches many journals rapidly using templates
rubrics_metrics.description: Begins operations with a large fleet of journals, often using a common template to quickly create each journal's home page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rapid proliferation of superficially similar journals suggests revenue-driven operations rather than scholarly curation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business management: insufficient or hidden information about author fees
rubrics_metrics.description: Provides insufficient information or hides information about author fees, offering to publish then sending unanticipated 'surprise' invoices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fees and timing should be stated upfront in Instructions for Authors or fee pages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business management: prevents indexing by blocking crawlers
rubrics_metrics.description: Does not allow search engines to crawl the published content, preventing the content from being indexed in academic indexes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check robots.txt and indexing behavior; deliberate blocking is suspicious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business management: copy-proofs/locks PDFs to impede plagiarism checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Copy-proofs (locks) their PDFs, thus making it harder to check for plagiarism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locked PDFs that prevent text extraction hinder quality-control processes; legitimate journals normally allow text mining for checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrity: journal name incongruent with mission
rubrics_metrics.description: The name of a journal is incongruent with the journal's mission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mismatch between title and scope may signal deceptive branding aimed at broad appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrity: journal name misrepresents geographic or institutional origin
rubrics_metrics.description: The name of a journal does not adequately reflect its origin (e.g., uses 'Canadian' or 'Swiss' when not related to those places).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check publisher location, editorial affiliations, and institutional connections to verify claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrity: false claims of indexing or indexing in non-indexing resources
rubrics_metrics.description: The publisher falsely claims to have its content indexed in legitimate abstracting and indexing services or claims indexing in resources that are not real indexing services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify indexing claims with named services and search for the journal in legitimate databases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrity: insufficient efforts to prevent author misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: The publisher dedicates insufficient resources to preventing and eliminating author misconduct, leading to repeated cases of plagiarism, self-plagiarism, image manipulation, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for plagiarism-screening policies, image integrity checks, and correction/retraction mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrity: solicit peer reviewers unqualified for manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: The publisher sends spam requests for peer reviews to scholars unqualified to review submitted manuscripts (specialties mismatch).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess reviewer invitations for relevance to expertise and check whether reviewer selection is sensible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrity: uses author-suggested reviewers without vetting
rubrics_metrics.description: The publisher asks the corresponding author for suggested reviewers and subsequently uses them without sufficiently vetting their qualifications or authenticity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper vetting of suggested reviewers is required to avoid fake or compromised peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other: republishes previously published papers without credit
rubrics_metrics.description: Re-publishes papers already published elsewhere without providing appropriate credits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for duplicate publications and appropriate cross-referencing or permissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other: boastful promotional language about status
rubrics_metrics.description: Use boastful language claiming to be a 'leading publisher' despite being a startup or novice organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promotional hyperbole should be verified against objective indicators of quality and longevity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other: uses a Western address/mail drop to masquerade as reputable
rubrics_metrics.description: Operates in a Western country chiefly to function as a vanity press for scholars in developing countries (uses a mail drop or PO box while operating elsewhere).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify physical contact details and staff locations; apparent Western addresses with opaque operations are suspicious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other: minimal or no copyediting/proofreading
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide minimal or no copyediting or proofreading of submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look at published articles for editing quality; pervasive typos and poor formatting indicate low editorial standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other: publishes non-academic content or pseudo-science
rubrics_metrics.description: Publish papers that are not academic at all (e.g., lay essays, polemical editorials, or obvious pseudo-science).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether content meets academic standards for methodology, referencing, and argumentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other: hides or provides only web-form contact, no location
rubrics_metrics.description: Have a 'contact us' page that only includes a web form or an email address, and the publisher hides or does not reveal its location.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legitimate journals provide clear contact channels (email, postal address, and often phone).

rubrics_metrics.name: Poor standards: copies authors' guidelines from other publishers
rubrics_metrics.description: The publisher copies 'authors guidelines' verbatim (or with minor editing) from other publishers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unique, accurate instructions reflect real editorial processes; copied guidelines suggest template-driven operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poor standards: insufficient contact information or misrepresented headquarters
rubrics_metrics.description: The publisher lists insufficient contact information, including contact information that does not clearly state the headquarters location or misrepresents the headquarters location.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm organizational details and physical offices; lack of clarity is a warning sign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poor standards: excessively broad journal scope to attract submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: The publisher publishes journals that are excessively broad (e.g., 'Journal of Education') to attract more articles and author fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overly general scope without clear focus can indicate quantity-over-quality motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poor standards: combines unrelated fields in journal scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishes journals that combine two or more fields not normally treated together (e.g., 'International Journal of Business, Humanities and Technology').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interdisciplinary scope is legitimate if coherent; check whether the combination makes scholarly sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poor standards: requires copyright transfer upon submission or retains copyright after charging fees
rubrics_metrics.description: The publisher charges authors for publishing but requires transfer of copyright and retains copyright on journal content, or requires copyright transfer upon submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should be cautious about surrendering copyright, particularly when paying fees; legitimate open access often allows authors to retain copyright with a license.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poor standards: poorly maintained website (dead links, misspellings, grammatical errors)
rubrics_metrics.description: The publisher has poorly maintained websites, including dead links, prominent misspellings and grammatical errors on the website.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Low-quality web presentation correlates with poor editorial quality but consider resource constraints for some LMIC journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poor standards: unauthorized use of licensed images
rubrics_metrics.description: The publisher makes unauthorized use of licensed images on their website without permission or licensing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check image attributions and licensing to detect unauthorized use.

rubrics_metrics.name: DOAJ seal: provide permanent identifiers (e.g., DOIs)
rubrics_metrics.description: To receive the DOAJ Seal, journals must provide permanent identifiers (eg, DOIs) in the papers published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DOIs support discoverability and persistent citation; absence is a negative indicator for open-access journals seeking recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: DOAJ seal: supply article metadata to DOAJ
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide DOAJ with article metadata.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accurate machine-readable metadata is essential for indexing and discoverability.

rubrics_metrics.name: DOAJ seal: deposit content with long-term preservation program
rubrics_metrics.description: Deposit content with a long term digital preservation or archiving program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of recognized archiving services demonstrates commitment to preserving the scholarly record.

rubrics_metrics.name: DOAJ seal: embed machine-readable CC licensing information
rubrics_metrics.description: Embed machine-readable Creative Commons licensing information in articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear licensing supports lawful reuse and aligns with open-access best practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: DOAJ seal: allow generous reuse under accepted CC licenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow generous reuse and mixing of content, in accordance with a CC BY, CC BY-SA or CC BY-NC license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permissive licensing signals openness and reuse; check the exact license terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: DOAJ seal: register a deposit policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Have a deposit policy registered with a deposit policy registry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A registered deposit policy clarifies preservation and reuse expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: DOAJ seal: allow authors to hold copyright without restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow the author to hold the copyright without restrictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author-retained copyright with clear licensing is consistent with many reputable open-access models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think. Check. Submit: personal knowledge of the journal
rubrics_metrics.description: Do you or your colleagues know the journal? Have you read any articles in the journal before?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Familiarity and direct reading of journal content are helpful initial indicators of legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think. Check. Submit: discoverability of latest papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Is it easy to discover the latest papers in the journal?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good discoverability through search engines and indexing supports legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think. Check. Submit: identifiable and contactable publisher
rubrics_metrics.description: Can you easily identify and contact the publisher? Is the publisher name clearly displayed on the journal website? Can you contact the publisher by telephone, email, and post?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear, multi-channel contact information is expected; inability to contact is a warning sign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think. Check. Submit: transparency about peer review type
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the journal clear about the type of peer review it uses?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descriptions should state whether peer review is single-blind, double-blind, open, etc., and how it's conducted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think. Check. Submit: indexing in services you use
rubrics_metrics.description: Are articles indexed in services that you use?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indexing in appropriate, recognized services improves visibility and signals acceptance by the community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think. Check. Submit: clarity about fees and what they cover
rubrics_metrics.description: Is it clear what fees will be charged? Does the journal site explain what these fees are for and when they will be charged?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Upfront fee information avoids surprise charges; explanations of what fees cover are a mark of transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think. Check. Submit: recognisable editorial board and its members' acknowledgement
rubrics_metrics.description: Do you recognise the editorial board? Have you heard of the editorial board members? Do the editorial board members mention the journal on their own websites?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify editorial members’ association with the journal by checking their profiles and personal/institutional web pages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think. Check. Submit: membership in recognized industry initiatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the publisher a member of a recognized industry initiative (e.g., COPE, OASPA) or another trade association?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Membership is informative but not definitive; verify active participation and adherence to members' standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think. Check. Submit: DOAJ listing for open access journals
rubrics_metrics.description: If the journal is open access, is it listed in the Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DOAJ indexing is a positive indicator but absence does not prove predatory status; DOAJ listing is not infallible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid relying solely on Beall’s list or single indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: WAME cautions against using prior appearance on Beall’s list as the solitary method for determining whether a journal is predatory or legitimate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beall’s criteria and lists had limitations and biases (e.g., mislabeling some legitimate LMIC journals); use multiple checks and context-sensitive judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a cumulative red-flag framework for assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess initial indicators (Beall-like features, DOAJ presence, Think.Check.Submit features) and then investigate website and policies for warning sign features; the more red flags present, the more hesitant one should be to consider the journal legitimate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: WAME’s algorithm encourages combining indicators rather than relying on any single criterion; assessment remains subjective and contextual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning sign: editorial board member unaware of affiliation
rubrics_metrics.description: Someone you know listed on the editorial board or journal staff, when queried, is unaware of their supposed affiliation with the journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contact listed members to confirm; unauthorized listing is a strong red flag.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning sign: no author fee information in Instructions for Authors
rubrics_metrics.description: No information as to whether there are author fees in the Instructions for Authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fee information should be explicit in author instructions or a dedicated fees page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning sign: peer review not mentioned in Instructions for Authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review is not mentioned in the Instructions for Authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence of peer-review description suggests lack of quality-control processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning sign: little or no information about editor/editorial board
rubrics_metrics.description: Little or no information is provided regarding the editor or editorial board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of verifiable editorial information constitutes a warning sign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning sign: journal office location missing or discrepant
rubrics_metrics.description: No location is listed for the journal offices, or location is very different than the location of the editors and editorial board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discrepancies between stated office location and editorial affiliations merit investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning sign: poor discoverability in internet searches
rubrics_metrics.description: The journal website is not easily accessible in an internet search (acknowledging possible legitimate lags for new or LMIC journals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Low discoverability combined with other red flags is suspicious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning sign: unusual or variable publication volume
rubrics_metrics.description: The journal publishes either an unusually small, unusually large, or markedly variable number of articles each year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessively high output without quality controls suggests potential predatory behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning sign: formulaic, non-specific solicitation emails
rubrics_metrics.description: You or your colleagues have received formulaic e-mail solicitations for submissions that do not specify an interest in particular projects or areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generic mass solicitations are characteristic of predatory publishers seeking volume.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning sign: promised turnaround times too rapid to allow real peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Promised routine turnaround times for review and publication are so rapid they seem 'too good to be true' and unlikely to encompass time necessary for true peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate stated timelines against realistic peer-review durations for the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning sign: unresponsiveness to contact attempts
rubrics_metrics.description: You do not receive a response to e-mail or telephone messages sent to the editor or journal office within a few days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poor or no communication is a practical red flag for editorial dysfunction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning sign: name very similar to a reputable journal
rubrics_metrics.description: The name of the journal is very similar to the name of a well-known, established journal with a good reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Naming mimicry (hijacking or look-alike titles) is used to mislead authors; verify ISSNs, publisher, and editorial leadership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning sign: atypical publication fees (much higher or much lower)
rubrics_metrics.description: The publication fees are atypical for the scholarly publishing industry (much higher or much lower fees can both signal problems).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret fees in the context of country/institutional norms; extreme deviations require scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning sign: difficulty locating articles in scholarly databases
rubrics_metrics.description: It is difficult to identify articles published in the journal when searching Google Scholar or other databases (noting that new or LMIC journals may face indexing lags).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indexing issues are a concern when combined with other suspicious indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning sign: missing author affiliations/contact info in published articles
rubrics_metrics.description: Information about author affiliations and/or contact information is not present in published articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complete author metadata is a basic scholarly standard; omissions raise questions about editorial rigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy requires correction/retraction and dispute resolution mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Legitimate journals should publish corrections/retractions and provide mechanisms for journals incorrectly identified as predatory to correct the record; predatory journals often do not publish corrections or retractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify presence and functionality of corrections/retractions policy and processes for dispute resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional action: assess quality in promotion/funding decisions, not only quantity
rubrics_metrics.description: Academic institutions and funders should scrutinize quality as well as quantity of publications—identify acceptable journals according to quality criteria rather than excluding all online journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions should develop and apply context-sensitive quality criteria and identify faculty involved with predatory journals when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and remediation as a standard for future initiatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Future initiatives to identify predatory journals should be transparent and objective, with mechanisms for correction and for predatory journals to improve practices and become legitimate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation systems should include appeals/corrective mechanisms and public documentation of criteria and decisions.
